transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah… I guess what brings me in is this constant restless feeling. Like I’m wound too tight and can’t quite settle down, even when I’m supposed to be doing something calm.

Like, I’ll be sitting in a planning meeting at work and everyone else seems fine, and I’m just… internally buzzing. Or even with things I actually like, like painting, or yoga — which is supposed to be relaxing, obviously — I still feel like I can’t fully sit with it. I don’t know if that makes sense.
Do these feelings ever come on as sudden surges of intense fear or discomfort that peak within a few minutes?

Um… I don’t think so? Not like a sudden wave of fear that hits and peaks really fast. I mean, I get uncomfortable sometimes, but it’s more like this ongoing revved-up feeling, if that makes sense.

Although “peak within a few minutes” makes me think of when I’m in a crowded store and everyone’s moving too slowly—sorry, that’s probably not what you mean. I don’t really notice it as intense fear, more just… I can’t settle.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about different parts of your life, even when there isn’t an obvious reason to worry?

I’m not sure I’d call it worrying, exactly. I mean, I think about things a lot — work stuff, whether an order is going to come in right, or if I forgot to answer an email — but it doesn’t feel like this big anxious spiral all the time.

Though, now that you ask, I do sometimes get stuck on little practical things, like if I’m in the grocery store and the line is taking forever, I’ll start thinking about all the other errands I’m supposed to do, and then somehow I’m thinking about dinner and whether I bought the right kind of coffee filters. But I don’t know if that’s “worrying” or just… my brain jumping around.
Have you ever had a period where you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

I’m not sure… I mean, I have nights where I don’t sleep great, but I don’t know that I’d say I need much less sleep and feel amazing or anything.

Sometimes I’ll stay up too late because I get caught up doing something, like looking at vendor catalogs or reorganizing something that suddenly feels important, and then the next day I’m still kind of wired for a bit. But full of energy in a way that stands out? I don’t think I’ve really noticed that.
When you were a child, did you often have trouble paying attention or staying organized?

Yes, I think so. I mean, I remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I was always popping out of my seat or talking over other kids. And I’d blurt out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question.

It’s funny, I can still picture those little folded notes in my backpack—my mother would find them when she was looking for permission slips, which I also probably forgot to hand in. But, yes, the main thing was I had trouble staying still and waiting my turn, especially in class.
Do you still often interrupt people or have trouble waiting your turn as an adult?

Yes… I do still do that, though I don’t always notice it right away. At work especially, if the junior buyers are talking through something, I’ll catch myself jumping in to correct a detail or add what I think before they’ve even really asked me.

It’s not like I’m trying to bulldoze them — I actually think I’m helping — but then afterward I realize I kind of took over the conversation. Waiting for the right opening is… not always my strong suit.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on a task, even when you want to pay attention?

I mean… sometimes, yes, but I’m not sure I’d describe it exactly that way. It depends on the task. If it’s something with a clear deadline or something I find interesting, I can usually stick with it.

But if it’s more routine, like going through spreadsheets or comparing the same kinds of vendor details over and over, my mind can wander. Then I’ll suddenly remember I needed to email someone, or I’ll start thinking about whether we’re overstocked on one item, and then I’m down some other little trail. Actually, that reminds me of last week when we had this whole issue with a shipment label—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

So… yes, focusing can be a little hard at times, but I don’t know how “often” I’d say.
Do these restlessness and interrupting habits cause problems for you at work or in your relationships?

Yes, it has, though I wouldn’t say it’s ruined anything. At work, sometimes I move too fast or jump in and then there are purchase orders that have to be corrected. My planning coordinator has started giving some things an extra look, which is helpful, but also a little embarrassing.

And at home… family dinners can get tense. I’ll think I’m just being engaged in the conversation, but then my husband or the kids will say I’m talking over people. Then I feel bad, because that’s not what I mean to do.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking things, like emails, orders, locks, or the stove, even when you know you already checked?

Um… repeatedly checking? I’m not sure I’d say that’s a thing for me. I mean, I’ll look at an email twice if it’s important, or if there’s a big order going out and I don’t want the wrong SKU or quantity—actually, SKUs can be such a pain when vendors change their numbering—but I don’t think I’m going back over and over once I know I checked.

Locks and the stove… no, not that I’ve really noticed. My husband is probably more the “did we turn that off?” person than I am. So I guess, no, not repeatedly in that way.
Did this restless feeling start after a specific stressful life event or change?

Kind of, yes. I don’t know if I’d say it started all at once, but it’s been noticeably harder to manage for… about two years, a little over two years maybe. Two years and a couple months.

That’s around when the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings. And then the whole night would get derailed, dinner would run late, my husband would be on the phone with them, or we’d be rehashing something someone said—sorry, I’m getting into the weeds.

But yes, that timing lines up. It got harder to keep a lid on the restless feeling after that started happening more.
When you feel wound up, is it usually because you’re worrying about something?

I’m not sure it’s always worry, exactly. Sometimes it is, like if there’s been some family thing hanging over the evening, but other times I just feel sort of revved up and I can’t really point to one thought.

It’s more like my body is already going, and then if there is something to worry about, it latches onto it. Does that make sense? Like I’ll be unloading groceries and suddenly I’m reorganizing the pantry because the cans are in the wrong place, but I don’t know that I was worried about the cans. I just… had momentum, I guess.
Do you feel this restless, hard-to-settle way even on days when there isn’t any family conflict going on?

Yes, I do. That’s actually kind of the thing that made me come in—because even on normal days, when nothing big is happening with family or anything, I still feel like I’m wound too tight.

Like I’ll be sitting in a planning meeting and I’m supposed to just listen, but inside I’m not settled. Or I’ll try to paint, which should be calming—I mean, I bought all these nice brushes and then half the time I end up fussing with where everything is instead of just painting—but the restless feeling is still there. Same with yoga. I’ll be in a pose and thinking, “Why can’t I just relax into this like everyone else seems to?”

So yes, it’s not only the conflict. That makes it worse, but the hard-to-settle feeling is there even without it.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different things?

I don’t know if I’d say “many different things.” I mean, I worry about things, sure—who doesn’t? But it doesn’t always feel like I’m sitting there making a list of worries.

Sometimes my mind jumps around, like work stuff, something at home, whether I forgot to answer an email—and then I’ll remember I need to pick up detergent, and somehow I’m looking up storage bins online. Sorry, that’s probably not exactly what you asked.

So… I’m not sure. I do worry, but I don’t know if it’s a lot of time worrying about lots of different things, if that makes sense.
Do you often find it hard to stop or control your worrying once it starts?

I’m not totally sure. Sometimes it feels hard to stop once my brain gets going, but I don’t know if I’d call it “worrying” exactly.

Like, I might start thinking about one thing and then suddenly I’m thinking about five other things, and then I’m up checking something or moving something around. But with actual worry… I guess sometimes I can distract myself, sometimes I can’t. It’s not very neat in my head, if that makes sense.
Would you say you worry excessively more days than not?

I’m not sure I’d call it excessive, exactly. More days than not… maybe? I don’t really track it that way.

Some days I’ll think, “Wow, I’ve been chewing on this one thing all morning,” but then other times I’m just jumping from one thought to another and it doesn’t feel like worry so much as… noise. Like when I’m ordering inventory and then suddenly I’m thinking about whether I left something on the counter at home, and then I remember a vendor email, and then—sorry, that’s not really answering.

I guess I don’t know. I do worry, but I’m not sure it’s excessive more days than not.
Do you often have trouble finishing tasks once the most interesting part is done?

I’m not sure. I mean, sometimes I do finish things, especially if there’s a deadline or someone’s waiting on me.

But once the “fun” part is over… I don’t know, maybe I drift a little. Like at work, picking out products or comparing options is interesting, but the follow-up details can feel kind of flat. Then I’ll remember something else I meant to check, and suddenly I’m in a totally different spreadsheet—or honestly, I’ll go refill my coffee and end up talking to someone about something unrelated.

So… yes? Maybe sometimes. I don’t know if I’d say “often,” but I can see what you mean.
Do you often lose things you need for work or home, like keys, papers, or your phone?

I don’t think that’s a big one for me… I mean, not that I’ve noticed in a way that feels unusual.

I have places I tend to put things, or at least I try to. My bag is kind of its own little filing system, though not a very elegant one. I did buy one of those organizer inserts once, and then I spent more time rearranging the organizer than actually using it properly—but anyway.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I often lose important things. Maybe the normal amount? I’m not sure where the line is.
Are you often easily distracted by things going on around you, like noises or other people talking?

I’m not sure. I mean, I notice things going on around me, like if someone’s having a conversation nearby or there’s a weird noise, but I don’t know if it’s more than other people.

At work there’s always some kind of chatter or phones or someone asking about an order, so it’s hard to tell what counts as “easily distracted” versus just, you know, normal interruptions. Sometimes I can tune it out, sometimes I can’t. And then I start thinking about whether I should’ve followed up with that person—well, not person, like a supplier—and then I’m off on that for a minute.

So… maybe? I don’t have a clear answer. I haven’t really paid attention to it that way.
Have you felt this restless, hard-to-settle way for as long as you can remember, even before the family conflict started?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, the family stuff definitely made me feel more on edge later, but if I’m honest, I remember being like this way before that.

In elementary school, I’d get notes sent home because I kept popping up out of my seat, or talking over other kids. And I’d blurt out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question—which, I remember thinking was helpful, like I knew it, why wait? But obviously the teacher did not see it that way.

Funny, I can still picture those little notes folded in my backpack… although I probably forgot to give them to my parents half the time. But yes, I guess the restless, hard-to-settle part was there pretty early.
Do you sometimes get so absorbed in something interesting that you lose track of time?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I can get into something if it’s interesting, sure, like anyone can. If I’m looking at products or comparing vendors, sometimes I’ll keep clicking through options longer than I meant to—then again that’s sort of the job, so I don’t know if that counts.

Time is funny, though. Like if I’m in a store display area, I can start noticing how they arranged everything, and then I’m thinking about why that color was next to that one, and whether it would work for our customers, and then I’m mentally rearranging shelves that aren’t even mine.

But losing track of time in a big way? I don’t know. I haven’t really thought of it as a problem, I guess.

I don’t know if I’d say “many different things.” I mean, I worry about things, sure—who doesn’t? But it doesn’t always feel like I’m sitting there making a list of worries.

Sometimes my mind jumps around, like work stuff, something at home, whether I forgot to answer an email—and then I’ll remember I need to pick up detergent, and somehow I’m looking up storage bins online. Sorry, that’s probably not exactly what you asked.

So… I’m not sure. I do worry, but I don’t know if it’s a lot of time worrying about lots of different things, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the core symptom is excessive, hard-to-control worry, which would favor generalized anxiety disorder over ADHD or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Do you often find it hard to stop or control your worrying once it starts?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about difficulty stopping or controlling worry, which is an anxiety-related symptom not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure. Sometimes it feels hard to stop once my brain gets going, but I don’t know if I’d call it “worrying” exactly.

Like, I might start thinking about one thing and then suddenly I’m thinking about five other things, and then I’m up checking something or moving something around. But with actual worry… I guess sometimes I can distract myself, sometimes I can’t. It’s not very neat in my head, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the core problem is generalized, excessive worry that would support GAD versus ADHD-related restlessness and distractibility or an adjustment reaction.
doctor.question: Would you say you worry excessively more days than not?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry more days than not, which relates to generalized anxiety rather than any listed ADHD symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it excessive, exactly. More days than not… maybe? I don’t really track it that way.

Some days I’ll think, “Wow, I’ve been chewing on this one thing all morning,” but then other times I’m just jumping from one thought to another and it doesn’t feel like worry so much as… noise. Like when I’m ordering inventory and then suddenly I’m thinking about whether I left something on the counter at home, and then I remember a vendor email, and then—sorry, that’s not really answering.

I guess I don’t know. I do worry, but I’m not sure it’s excessive more days than not.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD from generalized anxiety/adjustment disorder by testing a core inattentive ADHD symptom that is not simply worry-driven.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble finishing tasks once the most interesting part is done?

target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty completing or following through on tasks after the interesting part is over, but the provided symptom profile does not include a task-completion/follow-through symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, sometimes I do finish things, especially if there’s a deadline or someone’s waiting on me.

But once the “fun” part is over… I don’t know, maybe I drift a little. Like at work, picking out products or comparing options is interesting, but the follow-up details can feel kind of flat. Then I’ll remember something else I meant to check, and suddenly I’m in a totally different spreadsheet—or honestly, I’ll go refill my coffee and end up talking to someone about something unrelated.

So… yes? Maybe sometimes. I don’t know if I’d say “often,” but I can see what you mean.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has broad inattention symptoms in adulthood to distinguish ADHD from anxiety- or stress-related restlessness.
doctor.question: Do you often lose things you need for work or home, like keys, papers, or your phone?

target_item.reason: The question is about often losing necessary items such as keys, papers, or phone, but the provided symptom profile does not include a losing-things symptom.

patient.answer:
I don’t think that’s a big one for me… I mean, not that I’ve noticed in a way that feels unusual.

I have places I tend to put things, or at least I try to. My bag is kind of its own little filing system, though not a very elegant one. I did buy one of those organizer inserts once, and then I spent more time rearranging the organizer than actually using it properly—but anyway.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I often lose important things. Maybe the normal amount? I’m not sure where the line is.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's symptoms are characteristic of ADHD by assessing distractibility from external stimuli, which helps separate ADHD from generalized anxiety disorder and adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Are you often easily distracted by things going on around you, like noises or other people talking?

target_item.reason: The question is directly about being easily distracted by external stimuli, but the provided symptom profile does not include a distractibility item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, I notice things going on around me, like if someone’s having a conversation nearby or there’s a weird noise, but I don’t know if it’s more than other people.

At work there’s always some kind of chatter or phones or someone asking about an order, so it’s hard to tell what counts as “easily distracted” versus just, you know, normal interruptions. Sometimes I can tune it out, sometimes I can’t. And then I start thinking about whether I should’ve followed up with that person—well, not person, like a supplier—and then I’m off on that for a minute.

So… maybe? I don’t have a clear answer. I haven’t really paid attention to it that way.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD from generalized anxiety or adjustment-related anxiety by clarifying whether the core restlessness is chronic and trait-like rather than primarily stress-linked.
doctor.question: Have you felt this restless, hard-to-settle way for as long as you can remember, even before the family conflict started?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept popping out of my seat, talking over classmates, and rushing to answer before the teacher finished the question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the restless, hard-to-settle feeling existed before the recent family conflict, especially whether it goes back to childhood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, the family stuff definitely made me feel more on edge later, but if I’m honest, I remember being like this way before that.

In elementary school, I’d get notes sent home because I kept popping up out of my seat, or talking over other kids. And I’d blurt out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question—which, I remember thinking was helpful, like I knew it, why wait? But obviously the teacher did not see it that way.

Funny, I can still picture those little notes folded in my backpack… although I probably forgot to give them to my parents half the time. But yes, I guess the restless, hard-to-settle part was there pretty early.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD from generalized anxiety or adjustment disorder by checking for hyperfocus, which supports ADHD when attention varies by task interest.
doctor.question: Do you sometimes get so absorbed in something interesting that you lose track of time?

target_item.reason: The question is about becoming absorbed or hyperfocused and losing track of time, which is not directly covered by any of the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I mean, I can get into something if it’s interesting, sure, like anyone can. If I’m looking at products or comparing vendors, sometimes I’ll keep clicking through options longer than I meant to—then again that’s sort of the job, so I don’t know if that counts.

Time is funny, though. Like if I’m in a store display area, I can start noticing how they arranged everything, and then I’m thinking about why that color was next to that one, and whether it would work for our customers, and then I’m mentally rearranging shelves that aren’t even mine.

But losing track of time in a big way? I don’t know. I haven’t really thought of it as a problem, I guess.
